products.name: AchatAI
products.card: A username, invite link or QR code can start a conversation without a phone number.
products.question: How can people connect without sharing a phone number?
products.intro: AChat makes the first contact a choice. I can point to its web and Android app, and to the three ways someone can find another person without exchanging a phone number.

sections.heading: What changes at the first invitation?
sections.body: A username, invitation link or QR code gives a person a way to reach someone they chose. That is a narrower request than handing over a phone number. The product also has anonymous rooms that can be opened without an account.

sections.heading: What can a visitor inspect?
sections.body: The released web app is the direct destination here. The roster also records an Android surface. I would check those actual entry points before describing a messaging experience as shipped.

sections.heading: Where is the boundary?
sections.body: The published facts describe discovery and anonymous rooms. They do not promise that every conversation is anonymous or that no information is ever stored. A useful portfolio page should keep that distinction visible.

sections.heading: Why keep these ways of meeting separate?
sections.body: A username, an invite link and a QR code all solve the first contact, but they ask different things of the people using them. The published release gives those choices alongside an anonymous room that does not need an account. I would inspect each entry point on the live web app, then check the Android surface recorded for the same product. The useful engineering question is whether a person can tell which kind of conversation they are entering before they share an address or start a room. The roster gives the routes into a chat. It does not settle every privacy question about the chat afterward.

products.name: CallVault
products.card: Record, find and export a call on Android; backup is a separate choice.
products.question: When does a call recording leave the phone?
products.intro: CallVault keeps the phone library at the centre of the experience. A person can play, search, annotate and export recordings there; private cloud backup is something they choose to enable.

sections.heading: What can the device record?
sections.body: The app records calls through the audio source a phone makes available. That qualification matters: Android devices and call routes differ, so the page should not promise a uniform capture result on every handset.

sections.heading: How is a recording found later?
sections.body: Playback, search and notes make a recording useful after the call. Export is an explicit action from the phone library rather than a reason to move every file to a server by default.

sections.heading: What stays under the user’s control?
sections.body: The roster says recordings stay on the phone unless private cloud backup is enabled. I would check that choice in the app before describing its data flow more broadly.

sections.heading: What deserves a separate decision?
sections.body: Backup does. The phone library already has playback, search, notes and export, so the recording can be useful without first moving it to a cloud account. Private cloud backup is a choice the person enables. That order is significant for an app handling call audio: a list of features is less useful than knowing where the file stays until somebody asks otherwise. I would inspect the backup control and an exported recording on the released Android app, then check the actual audio source on the device being used. The published product cannot make every handset supply the same source.

products.name: Capacitor Auth Manager
products.card: One Google sign-in call across web, Android and iOS, without a Firebase dependency.
products.question: How much sign-in code should three app targets share?
products.intro: Capacitor Auth Manager is a package I can inspect as code and on npm. Its current public contract offers one Google sign-in call for web, Android and iOS.

sections.heading: What does the package put behind one call?
sections.body: The package spans a browser and two native app targets. That gives a product team one public entry point for Google sign-in while the platform behaviour remains inside the package.

sections.heading: What dependency does it avoid?
sections.body: Firebase is not required as a dependency. That is a concrete integration boundary, not a promise about every application that might use the package.

sections.heading: Which provider is actually present?
sections.body: Google is the only enabled provider in version 3.x. I would rather name the available path than imply a menu of providers that the release does not contain.

sections.heading: How would I judge this package?
sections.body: I would start with the public Google sign-in call and follow it on web, Android and iOS, rather than infer platform support from one successful browser demo. The release says Firebase is not required as a dependency and that Google is the only enabled provider in version 3.x. Those are useful, testable limits. A team adopting the package still has to configure its own application and inspect the returned session on each target. The package is responsible for a consistent entry point; the consuming product remains responsible for its sign-in experience, account rules and what happens after authentication succeeds.

products.name: ClearHire
products.card: A structured profile feeds an ATS-friendly resume and employment checks.
products.question: What evidence can sit behind a resume?
products.intro: ClearHire brings resume writing and work-history verification into one career workflow. Its structured profile is the starting record rather than a pile of separately edited copies.

sections.heading: How is the resume assembled?
sections.body: The product has an ATS-friendly builder with structured profiles. Its career tools include bullet writing and ATS checks; the roster records 50 or more tools, not an outcome guarantee for a job search.

sections.heading: What adds trust to work history?
sections.body: Verified-employment workflows attach a checkable process to a claim; an employer still judges it.

sections.heading: What can be opened now?
sections.body: The released product is linked directly. A hiring manager can inspect its actual resume and profile flow before deciding what the claims mean in practice.

sections.heading: What could a candidate inspect?
sections.body: A candidate can begin with a structured profile, turn that record into an ATS-friendly resume and use tools such as bullet writing and ATS checks. The published count is more than fifty career tools, but that number says little about whether a particular resume states the right work. The verified-employment workflow is another inspectable step: it adds a way to check a claim without making the hiring decision for an employer. I would follow one profile through its resume output and then inspect what a verification actually shows. The product can make evidence easier to present. It cannot promise a job offer.

products.name: Eat This
products.card: Search food by nutrient, feeling or time, then see one serving’s contribution.
products.question: What does one serving actually provide?
products.intro: Eat This starts with the way a person is choosing food: a nutrient, a feeling or a time of day. The result is grounded in a serving rather than an unexplained recommendation.

sections.heading: How does the search begin?
sections.body: Someone can search by nutrient, feeling or time of day. That makes three distinct ways into the same food choice, without requiring the person to know a food name first.

sections.heading: What does the result quantify?
sections.body: The app shows how much of a nutrient one serving gives and identifies a cheap pick. A serving is the unit that lets a person compare a result with what they might actually eat.

sections.heading: Where does the app stop?
sections.body: Food search flags when a question belongs with a doctor; it does not give medical advice.

sections.heading: What makes a food result usable?
sections.body: The serving size makes it comparable. A nutrient amount without a serving leaves the reader guessing what the number refers to; this app ties the contribution to one serving and can point to a cheap pick. The search itself starts from a nutrient, a feeling or the time of day, which are three ordinary ways a person might arrive without a food name. I would inspect a result reached from each route and read the quantity it shows. When the question belongs with a doctor, the product says so. That boundary matters more than adding a confident sentence the food data cannot support.

products.name: Empora
products.card: A WooCommerce merchant can turn on the store modules they need.
products.question: Can a store install one plugin without adopting every module?
products.intro: Empora groups WooCommerce modules in one WordPress plugin. The useful choice is at the merchant’s end: which modules to switch on for that store.

sections.heading: What does the plugin contain?
sections.body: The released product puts store modules in one plugin. The roster does not enumerate each module here, so I would send a merchant to the live product for its current list.

sections.heading: Where does configuration happen?
sections.body: A web dashboard handles licences and optional store connections. That makes the plugin and the management surface two parts of the same released workflow.

sections.heading: Which decision stays with the merchant?
sections.body: Modules can be switched on selectively. That is a more useful description than assuming every WooCommerce store wants the same set of additions.

sections.heading: Where does the choice of scope live?
sections.body: With the merchant. Empora packages WooCommerce modules together, but it lets a store switch on the modules it needs rather than treating the whole catalogue as one mandatory installation. The web dashboard has a separate job: it manages licences and optional store connections. I would inspect those two surfaces together, because an enabled module and a configured connection are different facts. The public roster does not list every module or promise that a particular store setup is supported. A merchant should open the current product list and check the exact module before planning a rollout around it.

products.name: HabitForge
products.card: A rope thickens with check-ins and frays where consistency stopped.
products.question: What does a habit history show when a streak breaks?
products.intro: HabitForge makes consistency visible as a rope. The mark changes with check-ins and also shows where a person stopped, which is more honest than showing only a successful count.

sections.heading: How does the record look?
sections.body: The rope thickens with each check-in and frays at a gap. The shape communicates a history that a single streak number would flatten.

sections.heading: Can the habit be social?
sections.body: The roster records friends, challenges and a leaderboard that a person can leave. Those are options around the personal record, not a condition for keeping it.

sections.heading: Where does it run?
sections.body: The current web and Android apps can be inspected directly.

sections.heading: What does the rope reveal?
sections.body: A thickening rope records that check-ins happened; a frayed place records a pause. Both are part of the same history. The social pieces in the release — friends, challenges and a leaderboard — surround that personal record, and the leaderboard can be left. I would inspect a run of check-ins with a gap, then check whether the visual still tells the truth without a contest attached. The web and Android surfaces are both recorded for one account. The portfolio can describe the visible metaphor and the released platforms. It should not turn a habit tool into a promise that somebody will keep a streak.

products.name: LabFlow
products.card: A laboratory result travels from draft through validation to release.
products.question: When is a lab result ready to leave the workflow?
products.intro: LabFlow joins patients, orders, samples and results in one laboratory system. Its meaningful boundary is the validation step between a draft result and a released one.

sections.heading: What is kept together?
sections.body: Patient and order records sit alongside samples and results. Billing, inventory and quality control are part of the published product too, so the result does not live in an isolated form.

sections.heading: What happens before release?
sections.body: The roster names a validation workflow from draft to released. That is the step I would inspect when assessing whether the software respects the way a laboratory works.

sections.heading: What does this page claim?
sections.body: It describes the product workflow, not clinical accuracy or a regulatory certification. Those would need their own evidence and are not supplied by a portfolio link.

sections.heading: Where is the consequential handoff?
sections.body: Between a draft result and a released one. LabFlow keeps patient records, orders, samples and results in one system, but keeping them together is only the starting point. The validation workflow is the point at which a result changes status and becomes ready for its next reader. Billing, inventory and quality control are part of the same published product, so I would also inspect how those records sit beside an order. The release record establishes that the steps exist. It does not establish clinical accuracy, laboratory accreditation or the rules a particular jurisdiction requires; those claims need evidence beyond a portfolio page.

products.name: LifeWell
products.card: Vitals, medicines, sleep and more can live in one personal health record.
products.question: Which health notes belong together?
products.intro: LifeWell gathers daily health records on web and Android. It covers vitals, water, medicines, sleep and nutrition, plus periods, fertility and baby milestones.

sections.heading: What can a person record?
sections.body: Measurements, routines and milestones live in one account, so a person can return to one record.

sections.heading: How many surfaces are recorded?
sections.body: Web and Android are listed, with sync across devices. I can link to the released product so a visitor can inspect that behaviour directly.

sections.heading: Where is the boundary?
sections.body: This is a record-keeping app. The roster does not claim diagnosis or treatment, and neither should a page about the engineering work behind it.

sections.heading: What belongs in one personal record?
sections.body: The published app brings vitals, water, medicines, sleep and nutrition together with periods, fertility and baby milestones. Those are different kinds of entries, so I would inspect how a person finds one later and whether the web and Android views agree after sync. The release record says the product works across devices; it does not say that every health question has an answer inside it. That distinction keeps a useful record from being mistaken for clinical guidance. The page can show the scope of the software and point to the working app. Decisions about diagnosis or treatment belong with a qualified professional.

products.name: linux-cleanup
products.card: Inspect cache paths and run a dry run before Linux cleanup removes anything.
products.question: What can a cleanup tool show before deletion?
products.intro: linux-cleanup names the paths it can remove, exposes its limits and runs a dry run before a real removal. The point I would inspect is the decision before the destructive action.

sections.heading: What can be previewed?
sections.body: The desktop app shows cache paths and its boundaries before a person runs a removal. The command line has scan and dry-run commands that never delete.

sections.heading: What ships on Linux?
sections.body: The roster records an x86_64 desktop app distributed as AppImage and .deb, plus an MIT-licensed command line available through npx. A real removal produces a receipt.

sections.heading: Which promise is deliberately narrow?
sections.body: The dry run is a preview, not permission to delete personal files. A cleanup product is credible when the exact path and consequence are visible before a click.

sections.heading: What should a dry run earn?
sections.body: A readable account of the paths that a real run would touch. The desktop app names cache paths and limits, while its command line provides scan and dry-run commands that do not delete. After a real run, a receipt records what happened. I would inspect a dry run before choosing any removal, then compare its promised paths with the receipt rather than relying on a broad word such as cleanup. The x86_64 AppImage, .deb and npx command line are all recorded release routes. None of those formats changes the central rule: a preview must be useful before an irreversible action.

products.name: macleanup
products.card: See a macOS cleanup dry run while personal folders remain outside its reach.
products.question: Which folders should a maintenance tool refuse?
products.intro: macleanup carries a macOS section catalogue and a real dry run. Its published boundary is unusually clear: personal folders are refused unconditionally.

sections.heading: What appears before removal?
sections.body: A person can preview the sections and run a dry run before changing the machine. That gives them a chance to read the proposed work.

sections.heading: What is excluded?
sections.body: Personal folders are outside the tool’s permitted targets. I would treat that as an implementation rule to verify, not a line of reassuring copy.

sections.heading: Where can it be inspected?
sections.body: The public repository shows the current macOS tool.

sections.heading: How would I test its narrow promise?
sections.body: I would inspect the current section catalogue, run a dry run and look at the paths it proposes. Personal folders are outside the permitted targets unconditionally, so that exclusion is a behaviour to prove, not a reassuring label to add after the fact. The product is for macOS, and the public repository is a place to read how its current release handles those decisions. A preview also gives a person time to stop before any removal. The portfolio should not imply that every file called a cache is disposable. The useful promise is the specific boundary the tool enforces. The real test is whether a proposed path outside that boundary is refused, even when a section name makes it look routine.

products.name: Native Update
products.card: A Capacitor web-bundle correction can ship while the next store build is prepared.
products.question: Which app changes can ship while store review waits?
products.intro: Native Update gives a Capacitor app a route for updating its web bundle over the air. It also covers store-update and review prompts; native code still requires a store build.

sections.heading: What changes without a store release?
sections.body: JavaScript, HTML, CSS and assets in a supported bundle can be delivered to an installed app. A native plugin or manifest change remains a new binary. That line decides which release path a developer can safely use.

sections.heading: How does a team manage a release?
sections.body: The hosted dashboard and management API accompany the open-source self-hostable backend.

sections.heading: What matters after delivery?
sections.body: An update path has to verify what it downloads and recover if a bundle fails. Fast delivery is useful only when the app can still start after the change.

sections.heading: Which release path does a change need?
sections.body: A supported web-bundle change can move through an over-the-air update; a native plugin or manifest change still needs a store build. That distinction is the first thing I would ask a team to identify before it publishes a correction. Native Update also includes store-update and review prompts, and the release record names both a hosted dashboard and an open-source self-hostable backend. I would inspect how an installed app receives and verifies a bundle and what it does if that bundle fails to start. A fast upload is not a complete update flow. The installed app needs a path back to a working release.

products.name: NetCage
products.card: Block one Android app’s Wi-Fi or mobile data while the rest of the phone stays online.
products.question: Can one app go offline without disconnecting the phone?
products.intro: NetCage controls network access for selected Android apps. A rule can target Wi-Fi, mobile data or both; the rest of the phone can stay connected.

sections.heading: What does a rule target?
sections.body: The selected app and connection type are the decision. That is narrower than switching off Wi-Fi or mobile data for the whole device.

sections.heading: Can rules repeat?
sections.body: Profiles group apps and apply rules on chosen days and times. The roster establishes the scheduling capability, while the live product shows how those choices are made.

sections.heading: What should a visitor check?
sections.body: A rule should make its target and effect clear before it changes connectivity.

sections.heading: Why does the target need to be explicit?
sections.body: A network rule can block Wi-Fi, mobile data or both for one selected Android app while other apps remain online. If the target is unclear, a person can mistake a per-app rule for a device-wide switch. Profiles add another layer: groups of apps can receive rules on chosen days and times. I would inspect both the immediate rule and its scheduled version, including how the app shows which connection type is affected. The roster establishes the available controls. The live Android product is where a visitor can check the confirmation and status the software actually gives before depending on a rule.

products.name: PregnancyPal
products.card: Week-by-week notes can leave the app as a doctor-friendly PDF.
products.question: How can pregnancy notes travel to an appointment?
products.intro: PregnancyPal keeps week-by-week information alongside a person’s own notes on vitals, symptoms, mood and appointments. A PDF export gives the record a form they can bring to a clinician.

sections.heading: What is recorded over time?
sections.body: The roster names weekly tracking, nutrition and exercise, plus vitals, symptoms, mood and appointments. Those records are useful because they can be revisited in order.

sections.heading: What does the export change?
sections.body: A doctor-friendly PDF can be shared outside the app. The person decides when to create that document and whom to show it to.

sections.heading: Where does the product stop?
sections.body: The app organises information. It does not replace a clinical assessment; that boundary should be visible anywhere its features are described.

sections.heading: What travels out of the app?
sections.body: A PDF made for a clinician. The product also records information week by week — nutrition and exercise alongside vitals, symptoms, mood and appointments — so the export has a sequence to carry rather than one isolated number. I would inspect what a person can select for that document and how the dates read once it is outside the app. The person decides when to make and share the file. Nothing in the release record turns the software into a clinical assessment or advice about a pregnancy. That is why the export is described as a record to bring to a doctor, not an answer from one.

products.name: RentParty
products.card: Pass one phone around, play a CPU character or open an online room.
products.question: How does a property game keep its place between sessions?
products.intro: Rent Party is a property-trading game that can be paused. The bank and deeds remain in place when players return, whether they chose a shared phone, CPU opponents or an online room.

sections.heading: Who can join a game?
sections.body: Players can pass one phone around, play against CPU characters or open an online room. Those are distinct ways to gather a table without changing the underlying game.

sections.heading: What does the game remember?
sections.body: The product handles the bank and keeps deeds in place on resume. That continuity is the reason a paused match can remain a match rather than becoming a new setup.

sections.heading: What can be checked?
sections.body: The released game is linked directly. A visitor can inspect the actual flow rather than infer rules from a screenshot of a board.

sections.heading: What makes a pause honest?
sections.body: The bank and deeds remain in place when the game resumes. That matters for all three recorded ways to play: passing one phone around, sitting opposite CPU characters or opening an online room. Without the state of the bank and ownership, a paused match would become a fresh setup wearing the old name. I would inspect the transition out of a game and back into it, then check whether each mode presents the same essential state. The release record describes the available modes and continuity. It does not claim a particular rules variant or an outcome for every match.

products.name: SMS App
products.card: Send single, batch or scheduled SMS from a registered Android device.
products.question: Where does a scheduled SMS actually leave from?
products.intro: SMS App uses a person’s own Android device to send messages. The published flows include single, batch and scheduled sends, with device registration and volunteer-pool management.

sections.heading: What is the sending device?
sections.body: The Android phone is the sending endpoint. That is a concrete architecture choice, and it changes what a user should check before relying on a scheduled send.

sections.heading: Which workflows are public?
sections.body: Single messages, batches and schedules are in the roster. Device registration and volunteer-pool management are also recorded, but this page does not invent delivery guarantees.

sections.heading: Where can the route be inspected?
sections.body: The live product is linked here. I would verify a send against its actual Android receipt, not treat a queued status as proof that a phone sent the message.

sections.heading: Where does a send become evidence?
sections.body: At the registered Android device, not at the moment a web page says a job was queued. The published product has single, batch and scheduled messages, plus device registration and volunteer-pool management. Those are meaningful workflows, but they do not by themselves establish delivery to a recipient. I would inspect the device status, a scheduled item and the resulting send record before describing a message as sent. The architecture makes the phone an active endpoint. That gives a user control over the sending device and gives the product a responsibility to distinguish a planned send from an actual one.

products.name: Strata Storage
products.card: One API reaches browser storage and native Keychain or Keystore.
products.question: What stays consistent when an app moves from web to native?
products.intro: strata-storage presents one interface over localStorage, IndexedDB, cookies and native storage. It has zero dependencies and supports web, iOS and Android.

sections.heading: Which layers sit behind the API?
sections.body: The browser layers cover localStorage, IndexedDB and cookies. On native devices, the package includes Keychain and Keystore support.

sections.heading: Why is one interface useful?
sections.body: A caller can use the same package across the app’s surfaces while choosing the storage layer that fits the data. The API contract is the part a developer can inspect on npm.

sections.heading: What is the published limit?
sections.body: The package docs distinguish persistence and security across storage layers.

sections.heading: What must stay visible behind one API?
sections.body: The storage layers do not all have the same properties. A browser can use localStorage, IndexedDB or cookies; a native app can reach Keychain or Keystore through this package. One interface is useful when the caller chooses the layer deliberately and can still understand where the data goes. The public package declares zero dependencies and support for web, iOS and Android. I would inspect the API documentation for persistence and security differences before storing anything consequential. A common call shape should reduce repeated platform wiring. It should not erase the different trust boundaries of those stores.

products.name: Tilawah
products.card: Recorded Tajweed and Tafseer lessons sit beside self-paced progress.
products.question: How does a learner return to a recitation lesson?
products.intro: Tilawah offers recorded Tajweed and Tafseer lessons with progress tracking. A learner can study at their own pace and book live one-on-one recitation sessions in their timezone.

sections.heading: What is available without a booking?
sections.body: The recorded lessons and progress record support self-paced study. The roster does not claim a particular curriculum length or learning outcome.

sections.heading: When does a teacher join?
sections.body: Live one-on-one recitation sessions can be booked in the learner’s timezone. That is a separate path from opening a recorded lesson.

sections.heading: What can a visitor open?
sections.body: The live site shows current lessons and booking.

sections.heading: What can a learner choose next?
sections.body: A recorded Tajweed or Tafseer lesson can be taken at the learner's pace, with progress kept across the lessons. A live one-on-one recitation session is a separate choice, booked in the learner's timezone. I would inspect those paths independently: one starts with opening a lesson, the other with choosing a time. The roster does not state a curriculum length or guarantee a learning outcome, so this page should not add either. The live product shows its current lessons and booking flow. A useful account of it leaves room for a learner to decide whether recorded study or a session fits the next step. The difference between opening a recording and reserving a person’s time should remain obvious at the first decision.

products.name: Trizlink
products.card: A branded short link and a link-in-bio page share one analytics home.
products.question: What happens after a short link is shared?
products.intro: Trizlink combines branded short links, link-in-bio pages and click analytics. Custom slugs and domains make the destination recognisable before a visitor follows it.

sections.heading: What does a creator publish?
sections.body: A creator can make a short link with a custom slug or a link-in-bio page. Custom domains are part of the published product.

sections.heading: What can they measure?
sections.body: The roster records click analytics. I would inspect the product’s current reporting before claiming a specific metric or attribution method.

sections.heading: Where do the utilities fit?
sections.body: More than 50 built-in utilities are listed, but the core link workflow remains the reason to open Trizlink. A utility count does not describe how a link resolves.

sections.heading: What does the link owner control?
sections.body: A creator can choose a custom slug for a branded short link, use a custom domain and publish a link-in-bio page. Click analytics then gives a way to inspect visits, although the roster does not define every metric or attribution rule. I would start by opening a short URL and following its destination, then inspect the page and its reporting in the live product. The release also lists more than fifty utilities, but a utility count does not explain whether a link resolves reliably. The recognizable address and the destination it reaches are the first claims a visitor can test.

products.name: Video Controls Plus
products.card: Frame-step, loop and annotate HTML5 video across sites.
products.question: What can a viewer do beyond pressing play?
products.intro: Video Controls Plus adds detailed controls to HTML5 video: a broad speed range, an A–B loop, frame stepping, audio boost, filters, screenshots and timestamped notes.

sections.heading: How precise can playback be?
sections.body: The published speed range is 0.1× to 16×. A–B looping and frame stepping give a viewer ways to repeat or inspect a small part of a video.

sections.heading: What can be kept from a moment?
sections.body: Screenshots and timestamped notes attach something useful to a point in playback. The roster also records audio boost up to 400% and colour filters.

sections.heading: How is it operated?
sections.body: More than 40 shortcuts are listed. The released extension site is the place to inspect the current controls and their settings.

sections.heading: What makes a video moment repeatable?
sections.body: A viewer can use frame stepping and an A–B loop to return to the same section, then keep a screenshot or a timestamped note from it. The speed range runs from 0.1× to 16×; audio boost and colour filters are other published controls. I would inspect the extension on an HTML5 video and check whether a shortcut reaches the action its label promises. The roster says there are more than forty shortcuts, but the count is less useful than a control that works on the page in front of someone. The current extension site is the direct place to inspect them.

products.name: Waylock
products.card: Keep chosen stops fixed while the rest of an Android route is reordered.
products.question: What happens to a planned route after a wrong turn?
products.intro: Waylock sits over Google Maps for drivers and couriers. A driver can hold chosen stops in place, order the rest and keep the chosen route visible after a wrong turn.

sections.heading: What is fixed before departure?
sections.body: Chosen stops can stay in place while other stops are ordered around them. That lets a driver protect a commitment without freezing every part of the day.

sections.heading: What appears after a detour?
sections.body: The chosen route remains visible beside an option to return or take a new route. A wrong turn does not silently erase the plan the driver made.

sections.heading: Where is the platform boundary?
sections.body: It is a planning layer over Google Maps, not a replacement for it.

sections.heading: What survives a wrong turn?
sections.body: The chosen route remains visible. Waylock lets a driver or courier hold selected stops in place while ordering the rest around them, then presents a choice to return to the old route or take a new one after a detour. I would inspect how those fixed stops are shown before departure and how the alternative appears when the road changes. The product is a planning layer over Google Maps, which is an important limit: it does not replace the underlying map service. Its value is in preserving a driver's decision while still allowing a new decision when the route changes.

products.name: windowsweep
products.card: Name every Windows cleanup path and run a dry run before removal.
products.question: What should a Windows cleanup receipt tell you?
products.intro: windowsweep is a Windows cleanup command line and desktop app. It names paths before touching them, has 30 sections and runs a real dry run without network calls.

sections.heading: What happens before a delete?
sections.body: A dry run lists what would be touched. Personal files are chosen row by row, so a broad category is not treated as blanket permission.

sections.heading: How can it be run?
sections.body: The published routes include npx windowsweep and a Windows desktop app. The command line needs no separate installer for the npx path.

sections.heading: What is the trust boundary?
sections.body: The documented dry run names paths and makes no network calls.

sections.heading: What does a receipt need to explain?
sections.body: Before removal, windowsweep names paths and runs a dry run across its thirty sections. Personal files are chosen row by row. That turns a broad cleanup label into a list a person can read and refuse. I would compare a proposed run with the result and check that the no-network boundary remains true for the local tool. The recorded release routes are an npx command and a Windows desktop app; both should make the proposed work legible before a real change. A convenient launcher is useful, but the path list and the user's choice are the parts that earn trust.

products.name: ZTools
products.card: Browser-based formatters, converters and generators in one searchable toolbox.
products.question: Where should a one-off developer utility live?
products.intro: ZTools gathers developer and creator utilities in one searchable browser toolbox. Its published set includes formatters, converters, encoders and generators.

sections.heading: What is the entry point?
sections.body: A person can search the toolbox for the utility they need. That is more useful than scattering small tools across unrelated product sites.

sections.heading: Where does the work run?
sections.body: The roster says the tools run in the browser and work offline. I would inspect a specific utility before making a stronger data-flow claim about it.

sections.heading: What stays consistent?
sections.body: Search and dark mode bring the tool catalogue together.

sections.heading: Why put these small tools together?
sections.body: A searchable toolbox gives a person one place to find a formatter, converter, encoder or generator instead of following unrelated links for each job. The roster says the work runs in the browser, works offline and has a dark-mode-first interface. I would open one utility, inspect its input and output, and then check the same flow without a connection before repeating the offline claim more broadly. The product link points to the current catalogue, which is more useful than promising a fixed count of utilities. A tool's job is to make one transformation clear and predictable, then get out of the way. The specific tool page should name its input limits and show the result before a person trusts it with another file.
